caseno: Jail Appeal No. 690 of 2004 with Criminal Appeal Nos. 2331, 2282 of 2004 and Death Reference No. 93 of 2004.
lawyer:
Md Khurshed Alam Khan, Advocate—For the Condemned-Appellant Sohel in Criminal Appeal No. 2282 of 2004 and the Appellant Hannan in Criminal Appeal No. 2331 of 2004. 
Md Shamsul Huque, Deputy Attorney-General—For the State in all the Appeals and in Death Reference No. 93 of 2004.
parties:
Sohel (Md) @ Sana Ullah and another ------ Condemned-Appellants
vs
State ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: The Criminal Appeal No. 2282 of 2004, at the instance of the appellant Sohel @ Sana Ullah, is directed against the judgment and order or conviction and sentence dated 29-6-2004 passed by Mr Md Shamsul Haque, Additional Sessions Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka in Sessions Case No. 329 of 2002 arising out of GR Case No. 396 of 2001 corresponding to Savar PS Case No. 62(4) 2001. The Criminal Appeal No. 2331 of 2004 and the Jail Appeal No. 690 of 2004, at the instance of the appellant Hannan, is directed against the self-same judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29-6-2004. By the impugned judgment, the learned trial Judge convicted the appellant Sohel alias Sana Ullah and others under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced him thereunder to death. By the said judgment, the Court below also convicted the appellant Hannan and the absconding co-accused Hanif and Mannan under those sections of the Penal Code and sentenced them thereunder to suffer imprisonment for life with varying amount of fine each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for a further period of 6(six) months. The Court below made a Reference to this Division under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for confirmation of the death sentence imposed upon the condemned-prisoner Sohel. 

 3. The prosecution version of the case, in short, is as follows: 

 5. The Investigating Officer of the case is Sub-Inspector Md Shawkat Alam (PW 4), Savar PS, Dhaka. He investigated the case by visiting the place of occurrence. During investigation, he examined witnesses and recorded their statements under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and procured the autopsy reports of both the victims. He also got the confessional statement of the accused Sohel recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Anyway, having found a prima facie case, the Investigating Officer Sub-Inspector Shawkat Alam submitted the charge-sheet No. 552 dated 22-12-2001 against all the accused under sections 302/201/34 of the Penal Code. 

 6. At the commencement of the trial of the case, the learned Judge charged all the accused under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code. The charge was read over and explained to the accused present in the dock, namely, Sohel and Hannan; but they pleaded not guilty thereto and claimed to be tried as per law. 

 7. In this connection, it may be pointed out that the accused Hanif and Mannan absconded from the very inception of the case and the trial as against them was held in absentia in accordance with the provisions of section 339B(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 8. The defence plea, as it appears from the trend of cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses, is that the accused are innocent and have been falsely implicated in the case out of oblique motives. 

 9. After hearing both the prosecution and the defence and on an appraisal of the evidence and materials on record and in view of facts and circumstances of the case, the learned trial Judge came to the finding that the prosecution succeeded in bringing the charge home and accordingly, he convicted and sentenced the accused-appellants and the absconding two co-accused by the impugned judgment as aforesaid. 

 13. Be that as it may, it is well-settled that the implication of an accused in the confession of a co-accused is not a substantive piece of evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act, 1872. In this context, we feel tempted to refer to the decision in the case of Bhuboni Sahu vs King reported in 76 Indian Appeals (PC) 147. In the said decision, the Privy Council observed: 

 "But a confession of a co-accused is obviously evidence of a very weak type. It does not indeed come within the definition of "evidence" contained in section 3 of the Evidence Act. It is not required to be given on oath, nor in the presence of the accused, and it cannot be tested by cross-examination. Section 30, however, provides that the Court may take the confession into consideration and thereby, no doubt, makes it evidence on which the Court may act; but the section does not say that the confession is to amount to proof. Clearly there must be other evidence. The confession is only one element in the consideration of all the facts proved in the case; it can be put into the scale and weighted with the other evidence." 

 14. In the same light, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Joygun Bibi vs State reported in PLD 1960 SC 313=12 DLR SC 156 observed: 

 17. Mr Md Khurshed Alam Khan has drawn our attention to the decision in the case of Ustar Ali vs State reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 43 = 3 BLC (AD) 53 in support of his submission that no conviction of the accused-appellant Hannan can be recorded merely on the basis of the confession of the co-accused Sohel. We have gone through the decision very carefully. It appears that our Appellate Division has followed the 'ratio' enunciated in the case of Bhuboni Sahu vs King, 76 Indian Appeals (PC) /47 and some other decisions in Ustar Ali's case. The record shows that the confessional statement of the co-accused Sohel was not brought to the notice of the accused-appellant Hannan at the time of his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure with a view to enabling him to offer explanations, if any, there against. Since the conviction of the accused-appellant Hannan is solely based upon the confessional statement of the co-accused Sohel, it is ex facie illegal. As no independent evidence is forthcoming on record as against Hannan, no useful purpose will be served by remanding the case to the trial Court for properly examining him under section 432 of the said Code. It has already been conceded by the State that Hannan's conviction on the basis of the confession of the co-accused Sohel is untenable in law. Accordingly, the impugned order of conviction and sentence of the accused-appellant Hannan is liable to be reversed. 

 18. Mr Md Khurshed Alam Khan next submits that the alleged judicial confession made by the condemned-prisoner Sohel was not brought to his notice at the time of his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure causing a miscarriage of justice and that being so, the impugned order of conviction and sentence of Sohel cannot be maintained. In support of this submission, he has adverted to the decision in the case of the State vs Monu Miah reported in 54 DLR (AD) 60. 

 20. In the decision in the case of the State vs Monu Miah reported in 54 DLR (AD) 60, it was held in paragraph 10: 

 "10. The Court below also found that the examination of the accused under section 342, CrPC has been perfunctory which has seriously prejudiced the accused as incriminating evidence or circumstances sought to be proved against the accused was not put to the accused during examination under section 342, CrPC causing gross miscarriage of justice. In the case of Mizazul Islam vs State 41 DLR (AD) 157, sandal which was the incriminating material sought to implicate the accused was not drawn to the attention of the accused at the time of the examination under section 342, CrPC and, as such, the same was left out of consideration. Accordingly, it was held in that case that incriminating evidence or circumstances sought to be proved by the prosecution must be put to the accused during examination under section 342, CrPC., otherwise it would cause miscarriage of justice to the great prejudice of the accused." 

 21. By the way, the decision in the case of Mizazul Islam vs State reported in 41 DLR (AD) 157 may be adverted to. In that decision, our Appellate Division has held, inter alia, in paragraph 21: 

 While the trial Court kept 342, CrPC in view it is unfortunate that one of the important items for linking up the accused with the crime, namely, the sandal was not at all put to the accused as a circumstances appearing in the case against him. In the similar case in Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh vs State of Punjab reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 637, the Indian Supreme Court considered the implication of such omission. It was observed "Unfortunately, in his examination under section 342 of the Code, no question had been put to Sarwan Singh about these shoes. It is not unlikely that Sarwan Singh may have offered to demonstrate that the shoes did not fit in with his feet. In any event, failure to give him an opportunity to explain the circumstances in his examination under section 342, CrPC justifies the defence argument that this circumstances should not be used against him." 

 23. Since the co-accused Hanif and Mannan are fugitives from law, we refrain from making any observation on the merit of the case as to their implication in the commission of the offence. 

 24. We think, the ends of justice will be sufficiently met if the case is remanded to the trial Court for re-trial from the stage of examination of the accused Sohel @ Sana Ullah under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and disposal in accordance with law. 

 25. Before we part with the case, we would like to make some observations about the judicial incompetence of the learned trial Judge Mr Md Shamsul Haque. He is, no doubt, a Senior Judicial Officer. We are really flabbergasted at his crass ignorance about the provisions of section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It appears that he examined the accused Sohel thereunder in a very mechanical, slipshod and cryptic manner. Being a Senior Judicial Officer, the provisions of section 342 of the said Code should have been at his fingertips. 

 28. From the foregoing discussions and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, the Criminal Appeal No. 2331 of 2004 and the Jail Appeal No. 690 of 2004 preferred by the accused-appellant Hannan are allowed. Accordingly, the impugned order of conviction and sentence, so far it relates to the accused-appellant Hannan, is set aside and he is acquitted of the charge levelled against him. Let him be set at liberty at once, if not wanted in connection with any other case. 

 29. The Criminal Appeal No. 2282 of 2004 taken by the condemned-appellant Sohel @ Sana Ullah is allowed and consequently, the Death Reference No. 93 of 2004 is rejected. So the impugned order of conviction and sentence so far it relates to the accused-appellant Sohel is reversed and the case is sent back to the trial Court on remand for fresh trial from the stage of his examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and disposal on merit in the light of the observations made in the body of this judgment and in accordance with law within 60(sixty) working days from the date of receipt of the records. 

 31. Let a copy of this judgment be immediately transmitted to the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Bangladesh Secretariate, Dhaka and the Registrar of this Court each for taking necessary steps for punitive action against the concerned trial Judge, namely, Mr Md Shamsul Haque, the then Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka for his gross inefficiency in dealing with, trying and disposing of the case by the impugned judgment.
